name: Spain
sources: GDP $535bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series ESP, 1990 — the same series the rest of this roster's 1990 GDP figures sit on (USA 5980, France 1270, Italy 1180, UK 1090 all match it). CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden: Spain's GDP at market prices in 1990 was 50.1 trillion pesetas (INE, Contabilidad Nacional de Espana), and converting that at the 1990 average market rate of 101.9 ESP/USD gives $492bn. The gap is the Atlas smoothing in the World Bank series, not a disagreement about Spanish output. Consistency with the rest of the roster is why the World Bank figure is the one entered.
Population 38.9m: the census of 1 March 1991 counted 38,872,268. Spain was the fifth-largest economy in the European Community it had joined on 1 January 1986.

TFP trend 0.009: Spain's post-accession boom was capital-deepening rather than productivity growth — real GDP grew about 5% a year from 1987 to 1990 on a gross fixed capital formation ratio near 25% of GDP, while total factor productivity growth over 1980-1990 ran under a point a year. This is the number that stops the model reading the boom as a permanent Spanish miracle, which is exactly what it was not: the peseta broke in September 1992 and unemployment went past 24% in 1994.

Inflation 6.7% and a policy rate of 14.7%: Spanish CPI rose 6.7% on the year in 1990 (INE), and the Banco de Espana held its ten-day repo rate near 14.5-15% through the year — the highest real rate in the ERM, held there to defend the peseta inside the wide 6% band it had entered on 19 June 1989. The high nominal rate against moderate inflation is the whole of Spanish macro policy in 1990 and is transcribed as such rather than smoothed.
Revenue 38% of GDP and gross public debt 43% of GDP: general government, AMECO/Eurostat basis. Gonzalez's Spain built a welfare state in a decade and paid for it out of a fast-growing base.

Public investment 5.0% and private investment 20% of GDP: the highest public capital-formation ratio in the Community, the Barcelona Olympics and the Seville Expo both due in 1992, and the AVE Madrid-Seville under construction.

Military 1.8% of GDP and a strength index of 16: SIPRI puts Spanish military expenditure at about 1.8% of GDP in 1990. Roughly 263,000 personnel, largely conscript, no nuclear weapons — Spain had joined NATO in 1982, confirmed it by referendum on 12 March 1986, and stayed outside the integrated military command until 1999. Indexed below Italy's 26 accordingly.

Stability 70 and authoritarianism 0.13: a democracy consolidated after the failed coup of 23 February 1981, with the PSOE returned for a third term on 29 October 1989. Marked below France's 75 because of the near-total general strike of 14 December 1988 and because ETA killed 25 people in 1990.

Separatism 0.10: Basque and Catalan nationalism, both electorally institutionalised rather than latent. Herri Batasuna, ETA's political wing, took 18.3% of the vote in the Basque autonomous election of 28 October 1990 and its elected deputies refused their seats in Madrid. Set above Italy's 0.05 and well below Yugoslavia's, which is the correct place for a strain that produces bombs but not a partition.

pop_growth_1990 = 0.2582%/yr. Compound annual growth of World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series ESP (Spain): 38,330,364 in 1984 to 38,827,764 in 1989 — the five years ending on the eve of the 1 January 1990 start date. See EconomyRecord::pop_growth_1990 in spheres-sim/src/data/mod.rs for why the window ends in 1989 and not with the single-year 1990 rate.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

ALL 48 OF THE 1990-ELIGIBLE TECHNOLOGIES WERE RULED FOR THIS NATION, one at a time, against a standard published per technology rather than per country. 12 were held and are listed below with their citations; 36 were refused. The refused ids are named at the end of this note so that a reader can tell a cell that was examined and refused from a cell nobody looked at - those are different claims and the schema would otherwise flatten them into the same silence.

RULED AND REFUSED, ids only (the reasoning for each refusal is held with the board that wrote it, one standard per technology): core_packet_internetworking, core_single_mode_fiber, core_carbon_composites, core_combined_cycle_turbine, core_pcr, comp_risc_superscalar, comm_fibre_optic_backbone, comm_geostationary_comsat, ener_seismic_3d_imaging, ener_horizontal_drilling, ener_gas_turbine_combined_cycle, matl_semiconductor_lithography, matl_industrial_robotics, matl_lean_production, matl_single_crystal_superalloy, matl_rare_earth_magnet, matl_stereolithography, aero_precision_munitions, aero_pulse_doppler_radar, aero_stealth_shaping, aero_quiet_submarine, aero_recon_satellite, bio_oral_rehydration, bio_conjugate_vaccine, bio_monoclonal_antibody, bio_automated_sequencing, tran_container_intermodal, tran_post_panamax_ship, tran_electronic_freight_documents, tran_high_speed_rail, agri_drip_irrigation, agri_conservation_tillage, agri_integrated_pest_management, agri_tissue_culture_propagation, agri_marine_aquaculture, agri_flue_gas_desulphurisation.

COLLISION RESOLVED. Two authoring boards ruled the same cell for this nation and disagreed. The tie-break is uniform across the whole roster and is not a preference between authors: the cell belongs to the board that owns the technology's domain in the registry, which for every non-core id is also its id prefix, and which both cross-domain authors published as their own deferral. agri_composite_membrane -> HELD (agriculture-environment said held, biotech-medicine said not held; resolved to the board that owns the Agriculture domain, agriculture-environment) matl_composite_structures -> HELD (aerospace-military said not held, materials-manufacturing said held; resolved to the board that owns the Materials domain, materials-manufacturing).

SECOND AUTHORING PASS, 2026-08-31, USE-SIDE ONLY. The first pass was correctly instructed to rule NOT HELD when unsure, and produced a defensible but ragged board: the convergence channel was reading that transcription's INCOMPLETENESS as this nation's IGNORANCE, and paying it to catch up to things it already had. A second pass therefore re-ruled the 31 USE-SIDE nodes against an explicit standard published before any nation was looked at, each limb written separately into every source string. LIMB A: a citable fact putting the technology in general commercial or public service across the OECD on or before 31 December 1989, asserted once per technology and identical for every nation. LIMB B: the nation is in the Advanced Set - 1990 OECD member AND World Bank high-income in the 1990 groupings AND one of the 29 authored majors: australia canada france germany italy japan netherlands spain sweden switzerland uk usa. LIMB C: a performed and RECORDED search for a named fact placing the nation outside that deployment; a silent limb C is a failed limb C. Where limb A failed for a technology the board said so and fell back to the first pass's named-artefact bar rather than granting on the class claim - which is why several second-pass refusals contradict the brief's own opening cut. THE SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE BAR IS UNCHANGED: producing a jet engine is still producing a jet engine, and not one of the 17 sovereignty-side ids was added, removed or re-reasoned by this pass. THE PASS IS ADDITIONS-ONLY - no first-pass grant was removed or weakened - and it was authored blind of model output, with the simulation never run and no CAGR, gap or instrument reading consulted. ADDED BY THE SECOND PASS FOR THIS NATION, 3 cells: bio_cross_sectional_imaging (health and agriculture board), bio_recombinant_pharma (health and agriculture board), ener_crystalline_silicon_module (energy and transport board). The refused list above has been reduced by exactly those ids and by nothing else; every other first-pass refusal stands untouched, and each new grant carries its own citation below.

LIMB A FAILS and is not used; granted on the named-artefact bar. LIMB B: Spain is in the Advanced Set (OECD member from 1961, high-income in the World Bank 1990 groupings, and one of the 29 authored majors). EVIDENCE E2, a named plant in the nation, dated, plus a named domestic producer in volume: Iberdrola commissioned SPAIN'S FIRST GRID-CONNECTED PHOTOVOLTAIC PLANT AT SAN AGUSTIN DEL GUADALIX, Madrid, IN 1984, at 100 kW - the installation Iberdrola's own published history of solar energy in Spain treats as the beginning of photovoltaics in the country. Isofoton, founded in Malaga in 1981 out of the bifacial cell work at the Universidad Politecnica de Madrid, began mass production in 1986 and supplied the grid-connected system at San Agustin del Guadalix, so the modules in Spanish service before the start date were also Spanish-made. Sources: Iberdrola Espana, 'History of solar energy in Spain'; Isofoton company history. LIMB C SEARCHED, AND IT RETURNED A REAL LIMIT WHICH IS RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN OMITTED: Iberdrola's own account states that this 100 kWp connection 'was the only one that the peninsula had for almost 10 years'. Spain therefore held exactly ONE grid-connected photovoltaic plant on 1 January 1990. DISCLOSED LIMIT: this is the thinnest grant this pass makes on this node - 100 kW against Germany's Pellworm at 300 kW, Italy's Delphos at 300 kW, Switzerland's roughly one megawatt of rooftops and the USA's 5.2 MW at Carrisa Plain. It is granted because it is named, dated, Spanish, grid-connected and paired with Spanish volume manufacture, and because the node is use-side and 'trivial as generation' by the registry's own description for every nation that holds it. A reader who applies a capacity floor rather than a named-artefact test should reverse this cell before any other on this node.

CASA manufactured the A320's carbon-fibre horizontal stabiliser, in service from March 1988. MODERATE CONFIDENCE, STATED: that attribution is the single leg this cell stands on. If it is wrong the cell should be withdrawn rather than re-argued.

Las Palmas III seawater reverse-osmosis plant, Gran Canaria, commissioned OCTOBER 1989 - four trains of 6,000 m3/d for 24,000 m3/d total, using FilmTec SW30HR-8040 THIN-FILM COMPOSITE elements, six per pressure vessel, in an 85:51 brine-staging array (Hydranautics / membranes.com technical paper, 'Las Palmas III, the Success Story of Brine Staging'). Named plant, dated before the start date, membrane chemistry identified by element model. This is the strongest single cell in my group.

Almeria: plastic-covered horticulture grew from 45 hectares in 1970 to tens of thousands of hectares by the 1990s on the Campo de Dalias coastal plain, the largest concentration of greenhouses in the world, later measured at 26,000 ha and 32,554 ha in Almeria province in 2020. This is the deployment the tree's own entry comment reads its 1990 floor off (spheres-sim/src/tech/agriculture.rs:91-95); see also NASA Earth Observatory, 'Almeria's Sea of Greenhouses'.
